title: Enums, flags & permission masks
description: The authorization bitmask toolkit: revoke / toggle, any-of vs all-of mask checks (and the vacuous empty mask), safe wire parsing (the Enum.TryParse "99" and comma-list traps), stable wire names, decomposition into names, popcount and the power-of-two test, role matrices. The enums ship in each drill's `// ─── types ───` section. Nearest existing units: jstrain-cs 09/* and csbootcamp 01/06 (pattern matching / switch expressions — mappings here use dictionaries instead) and csbootcamp 01/09 (boxing and enum equality theory).

exercises.title: Revoke and toggle rights
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "An admin removes Write from a user. Someone wrote `p ^ Perm.Write`. What happens to a user who never had Write?"

**Contract.** `Revoke` clears every bit of `remove` and leaves all other bits alone; revoking a right the user does not hold changes nothing. `Toggle` flips the bits of `flag`: held → removed, absent → granted. (That second half is why XOR is the WRONG tool for revocation.)

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `Perm Revoke(Perm p, Perm remove)` → `p` with every right in `remove` cleared and every other right untouched
- `Perm Toggle(Perm p, Perm flag)` → `p` with each right in `flag` flipped: held becomes removed, absent becomes granted

**Worked example.** `Revoke(Perm.Admin, Perm.Write)` → 0b111 & ~0b010 = 0b101 → **Read | Delete**.
exercises.explanation:
AND with the complement keeps exactly the bits that `remove` does not name.

For `Revoke(Perm.Admin, Perm.Write)`:
- Admin = 0b111, ~Write = …11101
- 0b111 & …11101 = 0b101 → **Read | Delete**
- `Revoke(Read, Write)`: 0b001 & …11101 = 0b001 — untouched, as required

XOR would have granted Write to a user without it; use and-not to remove, XOR only when you really mean flip.
hints: Removing must be safe for rights the user does not have — which bit operation can only ever clear bits?
p & ~remove clears the named bits; p ^ flag flips them.
Removal is and-with-complement which safely ignores rights not held, while toggle is exclusive-or which flips the named bits whichever state they were in

exercises.title: Any-of vs all-of mask checks
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "An endpoint is annotated with a mask of rights. Write both policies — 'any of these rights' and 'all of these rights' — and tell me what each says for an empty mask."

**Contract.** `HasAny` is true when `p` and `mask` share at least one bit. `HasAll` is true when every bit of `mask` is in `p`. With `mask == Perm.None`, `HasAny` is **false** (no shared bit) and `HasAll` is **true** — the empty requirement is vacuously satisfied. That is exactly what `p.HasFlag(Perm.None)` returns too, and why a policy built from an accidentally empty mask lets everyone in.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `bool HasAny(Perm p, Perm mask)` → true when `p` holds at least one right of `mask`
- `bool HasAll(Perm p, Perm mask)` → true when `p` holds every right of `mask`

**Worked example.** `p = Read | Write`, `mask = Write | Delete` → intersection 0b010: `HasAny` **true**, `HasAll` **false** (Delete missing).
exercises.explanation:
Both checks start from the same intersection `p & mask`; they differ in what they demand of it.

For `p = Read | Write` (0b011), `mask = Write | Delete` (0b110):
- `p & mask` = 0b010
- any-of: 0b010 ≠ 0 → **true**
- all-of: 0b010 == 0b110? no → **false**

With an empty mask the intersection is 0 and equals the mask, so all-of passes vacuously — treat `Perm.None` requirements deliberately.
hints: Both questions start from the bits p and mask have in common — then ask what you require of that overlap.
any-of: (p & mask) != 0; all-of: (p & mask) == mask. Try mask = None in both.
Any-of is a nonzero intersection while all-of demands the intersection give back the whole mask — an empty mask makes all-of vacuously true, so handle the none mask deliberately

exercises.title: Parse a status safely (the TryParse("99") trap)
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A webhook sends `status=99`. Your handler does `Enum.TryParse<OrderStatus>(s, out var st)` and it returns true. What did you just store?"

**Contract.** `OrderStatus` (given) is `Pending = 0, Paid = 1, Shipped = 2, Cancelled = 3`. Accept a member NAME in any letter case, or a digit string that names a declared value (`"2"` → `Shipped`; the tests pin that). Everything else is `null`: unknown names, empty input, undeclared numbers — and comma lists.

`Enum.TryParse` is not a safe parser at a trust boundary, for two reasons. It accepts ANY integer text: `"99"` succeeds and yields `(OrderStatus)99`, a value no member declares. And it accepts a comma-separated list of names and ORs them together, for every enum, `[Flags]` or not: `"paid,shipped"` parses as 1 | 2 = 3 = `Cancelled`, which `Enum.IsDefined` then confirms. A defined-value check catches the first trap, never the second.

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `OrderStatus? ParseStatus(string s)` → the status `s` names exactly (a name in any case, or a declared number in digits), else `null`

**Worked example.** `ParseStatus("99")` → TryParse true with value 99 → not defined → **null**.
exercises.explanation:
`Enum.TryParse` answers "is this text a name or a number?", not "is this one of my members?" — enums are just integers underneath.

For `ParseStatus("99")`:
- TryParse → true, value `(OrderStatus)99`
- `Enum.IsDefined` → no member has value 99 → false
- → **null**

For `ParseStatus("paid,shipped")`, TryParse is worse: it ORs the names into 1 | 2 = 3, a DECLARED value (`Cancelled`), so the `IsDefined` guard passes and a webhook has just cancelled an order it meant to mark paid. That is why the reference never calls TryParse: it accepts a digit string only when the number is declared, and otherwise an exact member name.

At a trust boundary, accept exactly the spellings you mean to accept — a name match like this one, or the explicit wire dictionary of drill 05 — and treat everything else as junk before it reaches your database.
hints: Enums are integers wearing names — what does TryParse do with text that is just a number?
Enum.TryParse is the trap; the safe pieces are Enum.GetNames<OrderStatus>, string.Equals with StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase, char.IsAsciiDigit and Enum.IsDefined.

TryParse happily accepts any integer text and even a comma list of names that it ORs into another member, so only an exact case-insensitive name match or a digit string that lands on a declared member becomes a status, everything else is null

exercises.title: Stable wire names for an enum
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Your JSON emits `status.ToString()`. A teammate renames `Cancelled` to `Canceled`. What breaks, and how do you stop it from ever happening?"

**Contract.** The API strings are `"pending"`, `"paid"`, `"shipped"`, `"cancelled"` — fixed, independent of the C# member names. `ToWire` maps a status to its string; `FromWire` maps back by EXACT (ordinal, case-sensitive) match. Any other string — including `"Paid"` and `""` — is a contract violation: throw `ArgumentException` with the message `unknown status '<s>'`.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions (declare the maps as top-level locals above them if you like):
- `string ToWire(OrderStatus s)`
- `OrderStatus FromWire(string s)`

**Worked example.** `FromWire(ToWire(OrderStatus.Shipped))` → "shipped" → **Shipped**; `FromWire("Paid")` throws `unknown status 'Paid'`.
exercises.explanation:
Two explicit dictionaries make the contract visible in code review and immune to refactors.

For `FromWire("Paid")`:
- the inbound map has keys "pending", "paid", "shipped", "cancelled" (default ordinal comparer)
- "Paid" ≠ "paid" → no entry → throw **ArgumentException("unknown status 'Paid'")**

`Enum.ToString()` couples your API to identifier spelling; an explicit map couples it to a decision.
hints: The wire strings are data, not identifiers — keep them in a table you control.
Dictionary<OrderStatus, string> outbound; invert it (ToDictionary(kv => kv.Value, kv => kv.Key)) for inbound; TryGetValue or throw.
Keep two dictionaries, enum to wire string and wire string back to enum, and treat any key missing from the inbound map as a contract violation worth an exception

exercises.title: Render a mask as its right names
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "`Perm.Admin.ToString()` prints `Admin`, but the UI needs one chip per actual right. Decompose the mask."

**Contract.** Walk the single-bit rights in declaration order — `Read`, `Write`, `Delete` — and include each one's name when `p` carries its bit. A composite such as `Admin` therefore expands into all three names; `None` yields an empty list. Composite members themselves (`Admin`) are never listed.

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `List<string> ActiveNames(Perm p)` → for each `f` in `[Read, Write, Delete]`, add `f.ToString()` when `(p & f) != 0`

**Worked example.** `Perm.Read | Perm.Delete` (0b101) → **["Read", "Delete"]**.
exercises.explanation:
Decomposing by single bits makes composites fall out for free: a composite is nothing more than several bits.

For `Perm.Read | Perm.Delete` = 0b101:
- Read (0b001): 0b101 & 0b001 ≠ 0 → "Read"
- Write (0b010): 0b101 & 0b010 = 0 → skipped
- Delete (0b100): ≠ 0 → "Delete" → **["Read", "Delete"]**

Iterate an explicit list of atomic flags rather than `Enum.GetValues`, which would also hand you `None` and `Admin`.
hints: A composite right is just several single-bit rights at once — list the atomic ones and test each.
Loop over new[] { Read, Write, Delete } and keep f.ToString() when (p & f) != 0.
Walk the declared single-bit members in order and keep each one whose bit the value carries — composites fall out naturally because they carry several bits

exercises.title: Count rights; is it exactly one?
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "`RequirePermission(Perm p)` must receive exactly one right, never a combination. Validate it — and count rights for the audit log while you are there."

**Contract.** Work on the underlying bits via `uint v = (uint)p`. `FlagCount` is the number of set bits. `IsSingleRight` is true when exactly one bit is set — the power-of-two test, where zero is NOT a single right. Write the bit trick yourself first; the framework one-liners are in the explanation.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `int FlagCount(Perm p)` → how many bits of `p` are set
- `bool IsSingleRight(Perm p)` → true when exactly one bit is set

**Worked example.** `Perm.Admin` = 0b111 → three clears to reach 0 → **3**; `IsSingleRight(Perm.Admin)` → 0b111 & 0b110 = 0b110 ≠ 0 → **false**.
exercises.explanation:
`v & (v - 1)` clears the lowest set bit: subtracting one flips that bit and every zero below it, and the AND keeps only the bits above.

For `FlagCount(Perm.Admin)`, v = 0b111:
- 0b111 & 0b110 = 0b110 (count 1)
- 0b110 & 0b101 = 0b100 (count 2)
- 0b100 & 0b011 = 0b000 (count 3) → **3**

A value is a single right exactly when one such clear reaches zero — and zero itself must be excluded first.

In production code, name the intent instead: `System.Numerics.BitOperations.PopCount((uint)p)` is a single hardware instruction on modern CPUs, and `uint.IsPow2((uint)p)` (.NET 7 generic math) is the power-of-two test, already false for zero. Both pass these tests.
hints: There is a classic bit trick that removes exactly one set bit per step.
v & (v - 1) clears the lowest set bit; count iterations until v == 0; a nonzero v with v & (v - 1) == 0 has one bit.
Clearing the lowest set bit with and-of-value-and-value-minus-one until zero counts the rights, and a value that is nonzero yet becomes zero after one such clear held exactly one bit

exercises.title: Effective permissions from roles
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A token carries `roles: ["viewer", "editor"]`. Given the role → permission matrix, decide whether the request may Delete."

**Contract.** The effective mask is the OR of the rights of every role name the matrix KNOWS; names the matrix lacks (a typo, a role deleted last week) are skipped and grant nothing — the system fails closed. No roles at all means `Perm.None`. `Authorize` is an all-of check: every bit of `needed` must be present in the effective mask.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `Perm Effective(List<string> roleNames, Dictionary<string, Perm> roles)` → the union of the rights of every role name the matrix knows
- `bool Authorize(List<string> roleNames, Dictionary<string, Perm> roles, Perm needed)` → true when the effective rights include every right of `needed`

**Worked example.** Matrix `viewer → Read, editor → Read | Write, owner → Admin`; roles `["viewer", "editor"]` → Read | (Read | Write) = **Read | Write**.
exercises.explanation:
Role composition is a fold with OR starting from `None`, and authorization is the containment check from the any-vs-all drill.

For roles `["viewer", "editor"]`:
- start None (0b000)
- viewer → | Read = 0b001
- editor → | (Read | Write) = 0b011 → **Read | Write**
- `Authorize(..., Perm.Delete)`: 0b011 & 0b100 = 0 ≠ 0b100 → false

Skipping unknown names (rather than throwing or defaulting to something) is what "fail closed" means in code: a missing role can only ever take rights away.
hints: Start from no rights and add each role's rights — but only for roles the matrix actually defines.
effective = None; foreach name: if roles.TryGetValue(name, out var r) effective |= r; then (effective & needed) == needed.
Fold the known roles together with bitwise or, silently skipping names the matrix lacks so unknown roles grant nothing, then authorize with the all-bits-present containment check
